voiceover: Here's a puzzle hiding inside the Gospels. When Jesus feeds five thousand, John says he turned to one specific disciple — Philip — and asked, 'Where are we to buy bread?' But why Philip? He wasn't the leader — that was Peter. He wasn't the treasurer — that was Judas. John raises the question and never answers it. Now watch. Luke tells the same story and adds a detail John leaves out: it happened near a town called Bethsaida. And John — five chapters earlier, for a completely unrelated reason — mentions in passing that Philip was from Bethsaida. Put them together and the puzzle dissolves: Jesus asked Philip because they were near Philip's hometown — he'd know the local markets. But no single Gospel says that. You have to assemble it yourself, from three details scattered across different books. This is an undesigned coincidence. People who invent a story together agree on the big claims. What they almost never fake is a tiny detail in one book that accidentally answers a riddle left open in another — with neither writer noticing. And it happens again and again. Luke shows Jesus' circle had inside knowledge of Herod's court — he could call the tetrarch 'that fox.' How would they know? Luke mentions elsewhere that one of the women funding Jesus was Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager. And Acts names Manaen, raised alongside Herod himself. Inside sources. William Paley and John James Blunt catalogued dozens; today Lydia McGrew calls them hidden in plain view. And that is very hard to square with the idea that the Gospels are late, free-floating legend. They read like the residue of real memory.
